description:
Wesam Saad examines why bodily resurrection belongs at the centre of Christian hope. Being with Christ after death is better than present life, but he explains that salvation also includes the future redemption of the body. Drawing on Genesis and 1 Corinthians 15, he presents human beings as embodied persons and answers objections based on Paul’s language about a spiritual body and flesh and blood. In this reading, resurrection transforms a mortal body into an imperishable one; it does not replace human existence with a disembodied spirit. Without Christ’s resurrection, Christian preaching, faith and confidence in forgiveness would collapse.

The risen Jesus provides the pattern for believers’ future bodies. Saad considers the empty tomb, Jesus being touched and eating, and his recognisable relationships with his disciples. He also explains how Christ as the firstfruits assures those who belong to him that they will rise, connecting this hope with the restoration of creation. Care is needed when drawing conclusions: qualities belonging to Christ’s divinity cannot simply be claimed for believers, and the discussion leaves the question of blood unresolved. The session closes with gratitude for Christ’s victory over death and encouragement to live now with the hope of a real, personal, bodily resurrection.

questions.question: What does this study mean by bodily resurrection?
questions.answer: Saad describes resurrection as a return to real physical existence, with the body transformed rather than discarded. Human beings remain embodied persons, instead of becoming permanently disembodied spirits. He grounds that continuity in God’s creation of humanity as body and spirit together.

questions.question: Why is resurrection still necessary when a believer is already with Christ after death?
questions.answer: The session distinguishes the blessed presence of Christ after death from the future redemption of the body. Reading Romans 8:23, Saad says believers still await bodily redemption because the promised outcome of salvation includes the whole person. He explicitly distinguishes that future outcome from Christ’s already completed atoning work.

questions.question: How does Saad interpret Paul’s phrase spiritual body?
questions.answer: He understands spiritual as describing a body governed and empowered by the Spirit, rather than a body made from nonphysical material. The contrast in 1 Corinthians 15 concerns mortality, weakness and corruption giving way to immortality and glory. Jesus’ risen body provides the concrete example behind that reading.

questions.question: Why does Paul’s statement about flesh and blood not rule out bodily resurrection?
questions.answer: Saad reads the phrase in its surrounding contrast between perishable and imperishable existence. The body must be changed because its present corruptible condition cannot continue into the kingdom. He emphasises that Paul speaks of transformation, rather than the destruction of embodied human life.

questions.question: What would be lost if Christ had not risen from the dead?
questions.answer: Following Paul’s argument, the session identifies preaching and faith as empty, the apostolic witnesses as false, and believers as still in their sins. Those who died trusting Christ would have perished, and Christian hope would extend no further than this life. Resurrection is therefore essential to the message being proclaimed.

questions.question: How does the firstfruits image assure believers of their own resurrection?
questions.answer: The first fruit belongs to the same harvest that follows it. Saad uses the image to explain that Christ’s resurrection is the beginning and assurance of the resurrection of those who belong to him. He connects this future hope with Christ’s reversal of the curse affecting humanity and creation.

questions.question: Which features of the risen Jesus support continuity in personal identity?
questions.answer: The study points to the empty tomb and to Jesus identifying himself, being touched, eating and continuing recognisable relationships with his disciples. These examples support Saad’s explanation that the person who rises remains the same person, with a transformed body. He presents that continuity as part of the hope believers can anticipate.

questions.question: What limits does Saad place on comparisons with Jesus’ glorified body?
questions.answer: Believers will be like Christ in their glorified humanity, but Saad warns against assuming they will share powers that belong to his divinity. He also declines to decide whether the resurrected body contains blood, while affirming the flesh and bones described in the account. Those limits keep the discussion from presenting every suggestion as established teaching.
